title: CMA finds private dentistry is ‘not consistently working well’ in interim report
html:
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has called for an overhaul of the UK’s £8 billion private dentistry industry as it released an interim report on its investigation into the costs of delivering private dental care.

Released today, the interim report found that around 60% of UK patients now pay for some private dental care, with more than one third doing so because NHS options are unavailable.

The CMA said the private dental market is ‘not consistently working well for patients’. Its concerns include affordability, weak price and quality comparison, workforce shortages, commercial incentives and regulatory gaps.

Prices at large dental groups rose by an estimated 7% annually from 2023-25 – which the report notes is ahead of inflation and wage growth. A composite filling was found to cost roughly 36% of weekly disposable income in the north east of England and 35% in Wales.

The interim report found that price variation was substantial even within local areas. For example, composite fillings are advertised from £80-£223 in Preston, and amalgam fillings from £72-£159 in Caerphilly.

The CMA also found potential conflicts between revenue incentives and patients’ interests, including evidence of targets to convert NHS patients to private care, sell higher-priced treatments and promote payment plans.

What improvements does the interim report suggest?

Examining dental workforce capacity, the report found that England’s estimated general dentist vacancy rate is about 8%, compared to 2% across the wider UK economy.

It also said that more than 5,000 dentists were waiting to sit the Overseas Registration Exam (ORE).

Several suggestions for improvement were put forward. These include:

  • Clearer treatment plans and record access
  • Better comparison information
  • Expanded training and scope of practice
  • Reduced barriers for overseas clinicians
  • Stronger business-level accountability
  • Governments using NHS purchasing power to encourage more affordable private essential care.

The full interim report can be found here. The consultation remains open to dental professionals and the public until 17 December 2026, with the full report due to be published by March 2027.

The role of mixed practice

The report says that the interconnectedness of private and NHS dentistry, including mixed practice, provides an opportunity for the government to shape the market and act in the interests of private patients.

It says: ‘The holding of an NHS contract could be linked to meeting those expectations; financial benefits flowing from NHS contracts could be increased for qualifying practices; and/or relevant practices could be granted kite mark accreditations or similar quality signals.’

The CMA said the next phase of its investigation would explore further how this could be achieved.

The report says recommendations to governments and regulators were more likely to improve outcomes than a formal investigation. However, the CMA said that it would be ‘premature’ to rule it out at this stage.

Who was consulted to inform the report?

Statutory information notices were issued to the four largest UK dental groups (mydentist, Bupa, Portman Dentex and Rodericks) accounting for around 15% of UK practices, along with 12 other large and 10 small to medium groups.

A notice was also issued to the National Association of Specialist Dental Accountants and Lawyers (NASDAL) to obtain anonymised financial information from roughly 500 independent dental practices.

In November, notices were also issued to more than 400 independent practices directly.

Seven large groups supplied treatment-level revenue and volumes, while others supplied estimates of what patients actually paid. Seven smaller groups and 105 independents supplied price data exclusively on composite fillings and tooth whitening. The CMA said these smaller samples were indicative, not representative.

Quantitative consumer research was carried out with 3,259 UK adults. The CMA held roundtables with dental groups, independents practices and consumer groups, and teach-ins with three of the largest providers, as well as directly analysing practice websites for pricing transparency.

Does the GDC support the interim CMA report?

The General Dental Council (GDC) welcomed the interim report and the fact it draws on its own research.

Stefan Czerniawski, executive director for strategy at the GDC, said: ‘Our Standards for the Dental Team require every dental professional to put patients’ interests first, give clear information about costs, including on practice websites, and get valid consent before treatment. 

‘Dental regulation is overdue for modernisation, and we have long been pressing for reform. Regulation has an important part to play but, as the CMA recognises, it is not a solution to the wider market challenges of affordability and access. We look forward to engaging with the CMA and the dental professionals we regulate to help shape the final report and recommendations.’

In August, the CMA wrote to the GDC in response to its new framework. It said:

‘We understand from your consultation document and our engagement with you that the intention for the new framework is to move away from detailed, rule-based standards and instead set out clear principles and expectations.

‘In the context of our ongoing market study, a particular area of interest for the CMA is how the new framework will provide clarity for professionals on what is expected of them to support informed consumer choice and decision making.

‘We are keen to ensure that our findings, and any recommendations we make for improving outcomes for consumers, can inform your ongoing work.’

How has the profession responded to the interim report?

The British Dental Association (BDA) said it agreed with the CMA that UK governments should use their power to shape the dental market.

BDA chair Eddie Crouch said: ‘Many make a positive choice to go private, and it is essential we have a thriving private dental market. But successive governments have left millions with no options when it comes to securing NHS care.

‘We know many patients are struggling. They deserve transparency, and we will work with the CMA on practical, proportionate steps to achieve that.

‘But when it comes to giving patients access to affordable care, ministers hold almost all the cards. The UK government can start by keeping their election promise, and fix and fund NHS dentistry.’

Simon Thackeray – board member, British Association of Private Dentistry

‘So far, the CMA’s opinions seem to be entirely based on the corporate sector, which has different economies of scale to a smaller independent practice. One can only hope the information provided by the 400 practices that have been asked will act to show the CMA that they only see one side of the equation currently – and it is a very skewed side at that.’

‘The CMA has not taken account of the increased pressures practices operate under: dental inflation of around 14%, higher national insurance costs and rises in the minimum wage. There is no comment on the lack of business rate relief for many practices as many are just too large to even qualify. 

‘It is also disingenuous to mention that one in six private practice websites have no pricing information – this means that around 83% of practices already do. 

‘What I am glad they have highlighted is the lack of an attractive NHS contract to work under, and the workforce issues, both of which as a profession we have been telling government for years.

‘The worrying aspects for me are the threat of price controls. This shows a complete lack of understanding of the different qualities of products that we can all use, from individual materials down to the price of the lab work. How can you control the cost range of something like a crown, when prices for the lab work alone range from £30 for a foreign import from China to more than £1,000 per unit from a local world-class technician?

‘There is no analysis of the effect of VAT or the competitive nature of staff recruitment. We need to keep salaries of our dental care professionals higher than minimum wage to value their work and commitment to the profession.

‘It’s clear to me that the CMA has been told what to focus on by its paymasters. However, the report does admit that some of the data might be skewed as there haven’t been enough independent responses.

‘The BAPD position is therefore that it is vitally important that the submissions requested by the CMA are received so the picture isn’t skewed towards the operating processes of the corporate dentistry sector.’

When was the CMA study launched?

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves first ordered the report in November 2025, which BDA chair Eddie Crouch then dubbed ‘utterly perverse’.

Reeves said ‘hidden costs, lack of transparency and overtreatment’ had impacted families in need of dental treatment. As a result, she wanted to see ‘urgent action’ to help reduce prices.

Crouch said: ‘The chancellor is singling out private dentists for doing what any business does: covering their costs, some of which are of the chancellor’s own making.

‘At the same time, she’s very happy to starve NHS services of vital funding. We’d remind her that profits from private care are all that are keeping NHS dentistry afloat.’

The investigation was formally opened in March 2026, with the CMA calling for both dental professionals and consumers to discuss subjects ranging from finding a dentist and understanding prices to knowing where to go if something goes wrong.

What motivated the investigation?

CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell said: ‘Going to the dentist is an important part of health and wellbeing, yet we’re concerned many may be uncertain about costs, availability, treatment options and what they’re entitled to. 

‘For some, turning to private dentistry is a choice – but for many, it’s a necessity. People need clear, accessible information at the right time so they can make the right decisions for themselves and their families.’

The CMA said it ‘recognises the dedication and professionalism of dental professionals’ and that the investigation ‘is not a criticism of clinicians or the care they provide’.

However, criticism of the investigation among the dental profession remained widespread. Dental business owner Rasnaam Tiwana said: ‘You do not change outcomes by lecturing individuals, but by redesigning systems. If we want dental care to remain affordable, we do not need more investigations into dentists. We need policymakers who understand how their decisions play out in real businesses.’
